target: Agent 1’s claim that a national-holiday Election Day would remove major scheduling barriers and enable more people to vote.
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably remove voting barriers for low-income workers because private employers are not required by federal law to give paid leave or paid holidays, and many retail and service workers would still have to work or take unpaid time off, potentially losing wages.

target: Agent 1’s broader argument that Election Day as a holiday is an effective voting-access reform.
objection: Research indicates that an election-day holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase turnout compared with other reforms; measures like state laws requiring employer time off for voting or automatic voter registration are more direct and reliable.

target: Agent 2’s implication that federal holidays do not meaningfully change workers’ schedules.
objection: Federal holidays commonly lead to school closures, reduced operations, or modified schedules in many workplaces, so many hourly and low-income workers would face less disruption and lower lost-wage costs on Election Day than on a normal workday.

target: Agent 2’s claim that low-income workers would still be unable to vote because holiday scheduling would not help them.
objection: Even if some costs remain, reducing school/work obligations on a holiday lowers both time and wage costs for hourly workers, making it more likely that schedule-constrained voters can cast ballots.

target: Agent 2’s suggestion that targeted reforms make the holiday unnecessary.
objection: Automatic voter registration mainly addresses registration friction, not the separate problem of having to attend work or school on Election Day, so it is not a substitute for removing schedule barriers.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday should be rejected because other reforms may be more direct.
objection: Scheduling barriers and administrative barriers are different problems; a holiday still meaningfully improves voting access by addressing the time/work-schedule barrier even if other reforms could help with other obstacles.

target: Agent 1’s claim that international precedent shows the holiday approach is feasible and workable in the United States.
objection: The OECD examples are not a good model for the U.S. because those countries typically have broader reductions in school and work obligations on election days, whereas a nominal U.S. federal holiday would not reliably produce those holiday-like conditions for many workers.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that most U.S. employers would reduce or change shifts enough for a holiday to matter.
objection: Because federal law does not require private employers to provide paid leave or to close, and many retail and service employers stay open and staff workers on federal holidays, many hourly workers would still face effectively unchanged schedules.

target: Agent 1’s assertion that there is no strong evidence the holiday approach is uniquely infeasible or harmful in the U.S.
objection: There is strong reason to think the U.S. holiday/weekend model would be harmful for cost-constrained workers, because many low-income workers would still face work obligations and lost-wage costs despite the holiday designation.

target: Agent 1’s claim that a federal holiday would reduce work-schedule constraints for low-income workers.
objection: In the U.S., a federal holiday does not guarantee paid time off or workplace shutdowns, so many low-income hourly workers would still need to work and would still face the effective cost of voting.

target: Agent 1’s suggestion that federal holidays generally mean most workers get schedule reductions.
objection: Federal holidays do not require private employers to close, reduce hours, or give paid leave, and many retail and service businesses remain open with scheduled workers, so federal holidays often do not produce workplace-wide shutdowns or full shift reductions.

target: Agent 1’s weak-negation assumption that there is no evidence most employers keep unchanged shifts all day on federal holidays.
objection: That assumption is false because there is evidence consistent with many employers keeping workers on essentially unchanged shifts for much of the day on federal holidays.

target: Agent 1’s claim that most hourly workers would see reduced disruption on a federal-holiday Election Day.
objection: For most hourly retail and service workers, a federal holiday does not reliably eliminate work or keep schedules unchanged, so the election holiday would not reliably reduce their lost-wage or unpaid-time costs.

target: Agent 1’s argument that holiday status would meaningfully lower the cost of voting for low-income workers.
objection: If workers are still scheduled for essentially their normal full shift on a federal holiday, then the holiday does not substantially reduce the lost-wage or unpaid-time cost of voting for hourly low-income workers.

target: Agent 1’s weak-negation claim that there is no evidence most employers keep unchanged, full-day shifts on federal holidays.
objection: The premise is not supported because most hourly workers in retail and service sectors still face full or nearly full shifts on federal holidays, so the scheduling-barrier claim is unreliable.
